lesson.title: Flipping a Negation Through And and Or
lesson.summary: De Morgan's laws give you a mechanical, always-correct way to rewrite the negation of a compound condition, turning awkward not-of-a-group expressions into clean, readable ones.
lesson.body:
Once you know the and operator, the or operator, and the not operator, a natural question shows up: what happens when you negate a whole group of them at once? Suppose a program should reject an order unless it is both in stock and prepaid, so you write a rejection check as not (in_stock and prepaid). That reads fine, but as conditions grow it gets harder to reason about a not sitting in front of a parenthesized group. De Morgan's laws, named after the nineteenth century logician Augustus De Morgan, give an exact rule for pushing that not inside the parentheses so each variable gets its own, individual negation instead.

The two laws are: not (A and B) is equivalent to (not A) or (not B), and not (A or B) is equivalent to (not A) and (not B). Notice the operator flips every time the not moves past it: negating an and produces an or, and negating an or produces an and. A common mistake is to assume the operator stays the same, writing not (A and B) as (not A) and (not B), but that is a different statement with different truth values, not a valid rewrite. The flip is not optional, it is the entire content of the law.

Trace the first law with real numbers. Let x = 15, and consider not (x >= 0 and x <= 10), which asks whether x is NOT in the range zero to ten inclusive. Evaluating directly: x >= 0 is True, x <= 10 is False, so the and is False, and not False is True. Now apply De Morgan's law: not (x >= 0 and x <= 10) should equal (not (x >= 0)) or (not (x <= 10)), which simplifies to (x < 0) or (x > 10). For x = 15, x < 0 is False and x > 10 is True, so the or is True. Both forms agree, and the rewritten version is arguably easier to read, since "x is less than zero or greater than ten" states the idea directly instead of describing it as the negation of being in range.

The second law works the same way in reverse. If a login should be blocked unless the username is valid or a guest pass is present, you might first write allow it when not (bad_username or no_guest_pass), and De Morgan's law converts that into (not bad_username) and (not no_guest_pass), meaning both conditions must independently hold. This connects directly back to truth tables: you can confirm either law by listing all four combinations of True and False for A and B and checking that the two sides always match, which is exactly what a truth table is built to verify.

In practice, De Morgan's laws matter most when you are debugging or simplifying a condition that starts with not and wraps a whole group in parentheses. Rather than mentally negating the group as a block, which is error-prone, push the not through mechanically using the two rules, flip the operator, and negate each piece individually. The result is usually shorter to read and much easier to verify against the requirement it is meant to express.
